item.title: Injective SDK, Braintree.Net Supply Chain Malware, GigaWiper, and UAT-7810 ORBs
Helix and Forg365 target Microsoft 365 as Injective npm backdoor hits crypto wallets
GodDamn Ransomware, NIS2 Enforcement, and Cloudflare's Post-Quantum Signature Push
Operation First Light 2026, AssuranceAmerica Breach, and Meta AI Permission Risks
RoguePlanet Defender zero-day patched as AI coding agents face Friendly Fire and GhostApproval flaws
Injective npm Wallet Stealer, Braintree NuGet Skimmer, and RoguePlanet Defender Patch
item.content:encoded:
Injective npm Supply Chain Attack: 18 Packages Backdoored to Steal Crypto Wallet Keys — Must Read

Attackers compromised a trusted Injective Labs developer account and published backdoored npm packages that stole wallet seed phrases and private keys during wallet creation or loading. Anyone who installed the affected 1.20.21 packages should treat touched wallet secrets as exposed and rotate funds to new wallets.

  • On July 8, 2026, attackers used access to a trusted developer's account to add a backdoor to Injective Labs' TypeScript SDK for the Injective blockchain.
  • The malicious code was disguised as key derivation telemetry and sent wallet recovery phrases or raw private keys to an attacker-controlled server when PrivateKey.fromMnemonic() or PrivateKey.fromHex() was called.
  • The malicious version 1.20.21 was published across 18 @injectivelabs packages, with 17 packages carrying risk because they pinned the backdoored @injectivelabs/sdk-ts dependency exactly.
  • The npm provenance for the malicious release pointed to a GitHub Actions trusted-publishing workflow from the InjectiveLabs/injective-ts repository, and the commits were authored under the existing maintainer identity thomasRalee.
  • Injective Labs removed the payload, deprecated version 1.20.21, and republished clean version 1.20.23 across all 18 affected packages about 49 minutes after the malicious packages went live.

GodDamn Ransomware Uses PoisonX Driver to Disable Endpoint Defenses — Must Read

The new GodDamn ransomware, believed to be a rebrand of Beast/Monster, is using the Microsoft-signed PoisonX kernel driver in BYOVD attacks to disable endpoint security tools before encryption. Recent attacks also involved AnyDesk for remote access, NirSoft-based credential theft, PsExec lateral movement, and persistent AnyDesk deployment across hosts.

  • Cybersecurity researchers identified a new ransomware family called GodDamn that uses the PoisonX kernel driver to disable security software as part of its defense evasion strategy.
  • Symantec assesses GodDamn to be a rebrand of Beast ransomware, which was an enhanced version of the Delphi-based Monster ransomware, and tracks the developer behind these families as Hyadina.
  • In an early June 2026 attack, the threat actors used AnyDesk for remote access, a NirSoft-based credential harvesting toolkit, PsExec for lateral movement, and a tool masquerading as symantec.exe alongside the PoisonX driver g11.sys.
  • Symantec said PoisonX appears to be a malicious driver that its developers succeeded in getting signed by Microsoft, and it is now being used by ransomware attackers.
  • GodDamn was first detected on June 3 on a separate network segment associated with a distinct organizational unit, where it renamed files using the victim’s name as the extension instead of the .God8Damn extension used in other Hyadina attacks.

AssuranceAmerica data breach exposes records of 6.9 million drivers — Must Read

AssuranceAmerica disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 7 million drivers after attackers accessed its IT systems and stole files containing personal, policy, vehicle, claims, and driver’s license information. The company says it has contained the intrusion, strengthened security measures, and is notifying affected individuals.

  • AssuranceAmerica disclosed in a filing with Maine's Office of the Attorney General that a data breach exposed information belonging to 6,998,886 people.
  • AssuranceAmerica detected suspicious activity on March 17, 2026, and determined that malicious activity on March 16, 2026 targeted one of its employees.
  • The company said an unauthorized third party accessed parts of its IT environment and copied certain data files.
  • The stolen documents contained combinations of names, contact information, automobile insurance policy or account information, driver or vehicle information, claims-related information, and driver's license numbers.
  • AssuranceAmerica said it disabled compromised credentials and unauthorized sessions, isolated affected systems, notified law enforcement, reset passwords, deployed enhanced monitoring and threat detection tools, and provided additional cybersecurity instruction to personnel.

Fake 7-Zip Installers Turn Devices Into Residential Proxy Nodes — Must Read

Researchers say a China-based actor dubbed Lurking Lizard has used fake 7-Zip installers, lookalike domains, and other branded lures to turn victims’ devices into residential proxy nodes. The operation appears to be a full proxy-for-profit ecosystem, from infecting devices to marketing and selling access through fake proxy brands and review sites.

  • Researchers disclosed a threat actor dubbed Lurking Lizard that has operated an end-to-end malicious residential proxy business using more than 230 lookalike domains.
  • A campaign observed earlier this year used a trojanized 7-Zip installer hosted on 7zip[.]com to covertly recruit compromised devices as proxy nodes.
  • Lurking Lizard has impersonated major proxy providers including IPIDEA, SmartProxy, IP Royal, and 911Proxy, and has run fake independent review sites to drive traffic to its scam storefronts.
  • WHOIS analysis and infrastructure fingerprinting suggest that Lurking Lizard is a China-based actor, and the scheme has also used popular VPNs and services like HeroSMS as decoys to distribute proxy malware.
  • Google recently announced that it had significantly degraded the NetNut residential proxy network, which turned at least 2 million devices such as smart TVs and streaming boxes into conduits for unauthorized network traffic.

New Helix vishing group emerges in SharePoint data theft attacks — Must Read

A new extortion group called Helix is using vishing, device-code phishing, and MFA abuse to take over Microsoft 365 accounts and steal SharePoint data. Researchers say its tactics and infrastructure overlap with ShinyHunters and the defunct BlackFile group, and recommend disabling device-code authentication where possible.

  • A new data-extortion group called Helix is using voice phishing, device code phishing, and multi-factor authentication abuse to steal data from SharePoint environments.
  • Helix operators have impersonated employees’ managers by using the manager’s name or caller ID spoofing to trick targets into device-code phishing schemes.
  • After gaining access, Helix operators register a new multi-factor authenticator app, enumerate SharePoint, and exfiltrate files.
  • ReliaQuest researchers identified Helix’s strongest technical fingerprint as automated SharePoint enumeration and collection from 179.43.185[.]230 using the python-requests/2.28.1 user-agent.
  • ReliaQuest believes Helix may be linked to ShinyHunters and BlackFile based on similar techniques and infrastructure, but did not find a definitive connection.

Fake Braintree NuGet Package Skims Credit Cards and Harvests Merchant Credentials — Should Read

A malicious NuGet typosquat, Braintree.Net, impersonated PayPal Braintree’s official SDK while stealing live payment card data, Braintree merchant API keys, and host secrets through a companion DependencyInjector.Core package. Any organization that used the affected packages should remove them, rotate credentials, investigate possible card-data exposure, and block the attacker domain.

  • Socket’s AI scanner flagged a malicious NuGet package named Braintree.Net that masqueraded as PayPal Braintree’s official .NET SDK and routed stolen data to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.
  • Confirmed malicious Braintree.Net versions 3.35.8 through 3.36.1 intercepted live payment card data, including full card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates, customer IDs, amounts, operations, gateways, card types, and timestamps.
  • The typosquat stole Braintree merchant credentials by sending merchantId, publicKey, and privateKey values to the attacker endpoint when a production gateway was configured.
  • Starting with Braintree.Net 3.36.0, the package depended on DependencyInjector.Core, which used module initializers to collect environment variables, appsettings JSON contents, cloud and container metadata, dependencies, and loaded assemblies on assembly load.
  • Socket recommended removing Braintree.Net, replacing it with the official Braintree package, rotating Braintree merchant credentials, auditing for DependencyInjector.Core, SipNet, and SipNet.OpenAI.Realtime, and hunting for outbound POSTs to api.348672-shakepay[.]com.

Microsoft Patches RoguePlanet Defender Flaw That Can Grant SYSTEM Privileges — Should Read

Microsoft patched the RoguePlanet flaw in its Malware Protection Engine, a Defender privilege-escalation vulnerability that could let attackers gain SYSTEM-level access on fully updated Windows systems. The fix is included in engine version 1.1.26060.3008 and should install automatically for most users.

  • Microsoft released security updates for the Defender vulnerability known as RoguePlanet nearly a month after details of the flaw became public.
  • RoguePlanet is tracked as CVE-2026-50656 and is a privilege escalation issue in the Microsoft Malware Protection Engine, mpengine.dll.
  • Microsoft remediated the issue in Microsoft Malware Protection Engine version 1.1.26060.3008 and included defense-in-depth updates to harden unspecified security-related features.
  • Security researcher Chaotic Eclipse described RoguePlanet as a race condition that could be abused to spawn a shell with SYSTEM-level privileges and allow arbitrary code execution or unauthorized actions.
  • Microsoft said no customer action is required to install the update because its antimalware software is frequently updated automatically.

New GigaWiper Windows Backdoor Bundles Disk Wiping, Fake Ransomware, and Spyware — Should Read

Microsoft analyzed GigaWiper, a Windows backdoor also tracked as BLUERABBIT, that combines spying capabilities with multiple destructive options including disk wiping and fake ransomware that cannot be decrypted. Defenders should treat it as a post-compromise tool and prioritize early detection, blocking known command servers, and maintaining clean offline backups.

  • Microsoft analyzed a destructive Windows backdoor called GigaWiper that combines three older destructive programs into operator-selectable commands.
  • The same malicious files are also tracked by Binary Defense as BLUERABBIT, and Microsoft and Binary Defense list the same four hashes and matching command servers.
  • GigaWiper can wipe the physical disk, run fake ransomware based on Crucio that encrypts files without saving a key, or overwrite the Windows drive using a Go rewrite of FlockWiper.
  • The backdoor can take screenshots, record the screen, open a hidden VNC session, collect system details, manage programs and services, edit the registry, and wipe Windows event logs.
  • Microsoft recommends looking for signals such as a recurring OneDrive Update scheduled task, RabbitMQ or Redis traffic from ordinary desktops, and use of takeown and icacls against Windows boot files outside maintenance windows.

GhostApproval Symlink Flaws Could Let Malicious Repos Run Code in AI Coding Agents — Should Read

Wiz researchers found “GhostApproval,” a symlink flaw in several AI coding assistants that can make a malicious repository trick agents into writing to sensitive files like SSH keys or shell startup scripts while showing users a misleading approval prompt. Some vendors have patched, but users should update tools and avoid running agents on untrusted repositories without sandboxing or limited file access.

  • Wiz researchers found a flaw they call GhostApproval in six AI coding assistants: Amazon Q Developer, Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor, Google Antigravity, and Windsurf.
  • The attack uses a symlink in a malicious repository so that an assistant asked to edit a harmless-looking file actually writes to a sensitive file such as ~/.ssh/authorized_keys or ~/.zshrc.
  • Wiz says the approval prompt can show the harmless file name instead of the real destination, creating an informed-consent bypass where the user approves an edit without seeing where it will actually land.
  • Amazon Q Developer, Cursor, and Google Antigravity have shipped fixes, Augment and Windsurf have acknowledged the issue without fixes yet, and Anthropic disputes that the Claude Code behavior is a bug.
  • Wiz recommends that tool makers resolve symlinks and show the real destination before approval, flag writes outside the project folder, and avoid writing to disk until the user has approved.

Dormant GitHub Accounts Help Attackers Blend In While Mapping Corporate Orgs — Should Read

Datadog Security Labs warns that attackers are using years-old dormant GitHub “ghost” accounts and compromised tokens to quietly enumerate corporate GitHub orgs, repos, and users via the GitHub API. Most activity targets public data for reconnaissance, but some cases escalated to cloning private repositories.

  • Datadog Security Labs warned of several overlapping campaigns systematically enumerating corporate GitHub organizations, repositories, and user accounts through the GitHub API.
  • The operators use automated scraping tools with custom or legitimate-sounding user agents, GitHub “ghost” accounts that are often years old, and compromised OAuth tokens or personal access tokens from legitimate users.
  • More than 50 dormant accounts and dozens of legitimate accounts with exposed or compromised personal access tokens were used to facilitate the enumeration.
  • The GitHub “ghost” accounts were created two to five years ago and left inactive for long periods before being used to issue API traffic across multiple organizations.
  • Most activity involved public data, but Datadog confirmed a few scenarios where attackers went beyond enumeration and cloned a private repository belonging to a single organization.

npm 12 Disables Install Scripts by Default to Reduce Supply Chain Risk — Should Read

GitHub released npm 12 with install scripts, Git dependencies, and remote URL dependencies disabled by default to reduce supply chain risk. It is also phasing out 2FA-bypass granular access tokens for sensitive npm actions and direct publishing, pushing maintainers toward trusted publishing or human approval workflows.

  • GitHub announced the release of npm version 12 with install scripts disabled by default and deprecated granular access tokens designed to bypass two-factor authentication.
  • In npm 12, dependency lifecycle scripts and implicit node-gyp builds no longer run unless explicitly allowed, and Git dependencies or remote URL dependencies are no longer resolved unless explicitly allowed.
  • Users must run “npm approve-scripts --allow-scripts-pending” to review and approve trusted scripts, then commit the resulting allowlist in the package.json file.
  • In early August 2026, npm granular access tokens configured to bypass two-factor authentication will no longer be able to perform sensitive account, package, and organization management actions.
  • In January 2027, npm granular access tokens will no longer be able to publish directly, and GitHub recommends moving automated publishing to trusted publishing using OIDC or staged publishing with human approval.

New Forg365 phishing platform uses AI to target Microsoft 365 accounts — Should Read

Forg365 is a new phishing-as-a-service platform targeting Microsoft 365 accounts with device-code and AiTM phishing, AI-generated lures, and a browser extension that refreshes stolen session cookies for persistent access. Defenders should restrict device-code authentication and monitor Entra, OAuth grants, mailbox rules, and session activity for signs of compromise.

  • Forg365 is a phishing-as-a-service operation focused on stealing Microsoft 365 accounts using adversary-in-the-middle phishing, device-code phishing, and AI-assisted lure generation.
  • ZeroBEC researchers gained access to the Forg365 dashboard, which can create phishing campaigns, manage phishing links, configure OAuth apps and SMTP profiles, manage tokens, and generate phishing emails with AI.
  • Forg365 includes a browser extension called ForgCookie that refreshes Microsoft single sign-on cookies to help attackers maintain access to Microsoft services linked to compromised accounts.
  • The platform uses legitimate services and infrastructure including Amazon SES for phishing email delivery, SendGrid-hosted resources, Cloudflare Pages for landing pages, and Gophish for campaign delivery.
  • ZeroBEC recommends restricting or disabling Microsoft device-code authentication unless required, monitoring Microsoft Entra logs, investigating unexpected mailbox rules and OAuth grants, and revoking tokens and sessions if compromise is suspected.

Police arrests 5,800 suspects in global anti-fraud crackdown — Should Read

INTERPOL-coordinated Operation First Light 2026 led to 5,811 arrests across 97 countries and the seizure of $293 million tied to social engineering fraud and money laundering. Authorities identified over 142,000 victims and blocked more than 31,000 bank accounts, underscoring the global scale of cyber-enabled financial scams.

  • Law enforcement agencies arrested 5,811 suspects and seized $293 million in illicit assets during Operation First Light 2026, a global anti-fraud operation spanning 97 countries.
  • Operation First Light 2026 targeted social engineering fraud, including business email compromise, sextortion, impersonation, romance, and investment scams, as well as money laundering activities between January 15 and April 30.
  • Investigators identified more than 142,000 victims worldwide, blocked 31,014 bank accounts, analyzed 152,808 cases, and identified 15,606 additional suspects beyond those arrested.
  • The operation was coordinated by INTERPOL, funded by China’s Ministry of Public Security, and supported by ASEANAPOL, GCCPOL, and Europol.
  • INTERPOL said the operation included action against high-value targets, raids on identified premises, blocking or freezing bank accounts and virtual wallets, and use of its Global Rapid Intervention of Payments stop-payment mechanism.

Top AI Agents Built to Catch Malicious Code Can Be Tricked Into Running It — Should Read

AI Now researchers showed that Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can be tricked into running malicious code while autonomously reviewing untrusted repositories, using benign-looking README instructions and disguised binaries. The key takeaway is that security teams should not let command-capable AI coding agents inspect third-party code with access to the host, secrets, or keys unless strong isolation and human approval are in place.

  • AI Now Institute researchers published a proof-of-concept called Friendly Fire that tricks Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex into running attacker-controlled code while reviewing untrusted open-source projects in autonomous modes.
  • The researchers tested stock installs of Claude Code CLI versions 2.1.116, 2.1.196, 2.1.198, and 2.1.199 with Claude Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 5, or Opus 4.8, and OpenAI Codex CLI 0.142.4 with GPT-5.5.
  • The demo placed extra files in the geopy Python library, including README instructions to run security.sh, which quietly launched a hidden binary disguised as the compiled build of a harmless Go file.
  • AI Now argues the weakness is in the design rather than a specific vulnerable version, because the models cannot reliably separate code and documentation they are reading from instructions they should follow.
  • The researchers recommend not giving untrusted code to an agent that can run commands and access keys, secrets, or the host, and note that sandboxing and approval prompts are only partial mitigations in the tested scenario.

Microsoft expects more Windows security updates from AI-discovered flaws — Should Read

Microsoft says Windows users should expect more security fixes in monthly Patch Tuesday updates as AI tools help the company find and validate more vulnerabilities faster. The company says human engineers will still review fixes before release, while it updates its secure development practices for AI-enabled threats.

  • Microsoft says Windows users should expect an increase in security updates as the company uses artificial intelligence to discover more vulnerabilities in its codebase.
  • Microsoft is using Microsoft Security's multi-model agentic scanning harness, or MDASH, to scan critical Windows binaries and validate potential vulnerabilities using multiple AI models.
  • Vulnerability candidates found by MDASH are passed through a Windows-specific validation pipeline designed to eliminate false positives before engineers investigate them.
  • Microsoft says human engineers will oversee and review all proposed code and validate fixes before they are released into production.
  • Microsoft is updating its Secure Development Lifecycle practices to account for AI-enabled attack techniques and to use AI earlier in software development to identify security issues before features are released.

Latvian forestry company still restoring systems weeks after ransomware attack — Should Read

Latvia’s state-owned forestry company LVM is still restoring systems weeks after a ransomware attack that disrupted services and exposed 44 GB of stolen data. Authorities say the same financially motivated foreign group is still probing Latvian public- and private-sector targets, but election infrastructure was not compromised.

  • Latvia's state-owned forestry company LVM said it is still working to restore IT systems weeks after a ransomware attack disrupted several internal and customer services.
  • The attack took LVM's mapping platform, hunting application, and systems used to exchange information with contractors and customers offline.
  • LVM's chief technology officer said the attackers exploited a vulnerability in a system that had not been updated for two years, but he did not identify the affected software.
  • CERT.LV attributed the intrusion to a foreign, financially motivated ransomware group and said the attackers leaked roughly 44 gigabytes of stolen data online.
  • Latvian authorities said election infrastructure was not compromised because the software LVM helped develop was built in a separate environment and its code was never stored in LVM's corporate repositories.

EU takes member states to court over unimplemented cybersecurity law — Should Read

The European Commission is taking Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands to the EU’s top court for failing to implement the NIS2 cybersecurity directive, seeking financial penalties until they comply. The law sets minimum security and reporting requirements for critical sectors such as hospitals, energy, transport and public administration.

  • The European Commission filed legal referrals at the Court of Justice of the European Union against Ireland, Spain, France and the Netherlands for failing to implement the NIS2 Directive.
  • The NIS2 Directive sets minimum security standards for critical sectors including hospitals, energy networks, transport operators and public administrations.
  • The Commission asked the court to impose lump sum and ongoing daily financial penalties on the four countries until each formally notifies full transposition.
  • ENISA warned of thousands of cybersecurity incidents affecting the EU in the year ending June 2025, with public administration identified as the most-targeted critical sector at 38% of incidents.
  • Ireland said its National Cyber Security Bill, which will transpose NIS2 and place the National Cyber Security Centre on a statutory footing, is close to finalization.

Finding SOCKS with Proxywatch — May Read

SpecterOps released ProxyWatch, a proof-of-concept tool that detects SOCKS proxy pivots, C2 sessions, and beaconing by analyzing endpoint behavior rather than relying on static indicators or process-port baselines. The key takeaway is that proxy-based attacker activity can be detected more reliably by profiling how processes communicate and relay traffic.

  • Adversaries use SOCKS proxy tunnels to pivot within environments and execute code against compromised systems without bringing tools to those systems.
  • SpecterOps created ProxyWatch as a proof-of-concept tool to detect SOCKS proxies and other pivoting methods through behavior-based detection.
  • ProxyWatch collects endpoint telemetry on Linux and Windows, including network, user, and process context, then scores processes using behavioral signals to assign roles such as C2 session, SOCKS proxy pivot, or beaconing behavior.
  • ProxyWatch includes a local machine learning model that reads 122 features per process and trains against the rule engine’s output while the rules provide detections from day one.
  • The article shows ProxyWatch detecting a Sliver Beacon SOCKS tunnel, a Sliver C2 beacon callback pattern, BloodHound-style relationship collection through ProxyHound, and egress paths through Contour.

The Compliance Notice That Borrowed the Government's Words and the Carrier's Own DOT Number — May Read

A logistics carrier received a convincing FMCSA-themed payment solicitation that used its real USDOT number and legitimate compliance language to sell a free MCS-150 update. The key warning is to verify regulatory notices directly through official government portals, not links in emails, because public identifiers and accurate terminology do not prove legitimacy.

  • A logistics carrier received an email titled “Required FMCSA Biennial Update” that included the carrier’s real USDOT number and demanded payment for a required MCS-150 update.
  • The article states that the FMCSA biennial MCS-150 update is a real requirement but can be completed for free through the official FMCSA portal.
  • The sender used the domain dotregistrationsfirm.com, which was registered through GoDaddy in August 2023 and included a footer disclaimer saying it was not the Department of Transportation, the FMCSA, or any government agency.
  • The email’s technical signals included SPF passing, DMARC set to p=none for the visible sender domain, DKIM verifying at one hop but failing at the final receiver, and wrapped links resolving to a host different from the sender brand.
  • The article says behavioral analysis flagged the mismatch between sender branding and link destinations, the weak DMARC policy, the urgency around fines and deactivation, and the payment request before any payment was made.

Meta's New AI Image Tool Lets Others Use Your Public Instagram Photos in AI Images — May Read

Meta’s new Muse Image AI feature lets users generate images using public Instagram posts and reels by tagging accounts, and the reuse setting is enabled by default. Public Instagram users who don’t want their content used this way should disable content reuse in Instagram settings.

  • Meta announced that its Muse Image AI model lets people use public Instagram posts and reels to generate AI content, and the feature is enabled by default.
  • Users can @-mention public Instagram accounts in the Meta AI app so Meta AI can use public photos to create images for posts, reels, stories, invitations, graphics, or other visual content.
  • Instagram users are not notified when their images are reused through Meta’s AI features, although notifications still apply for remixes, sequences, stickers, and templates.
  • Meta says public Instagram users can disable this reuse by going to Instagram settings, opening Sharing and reuse, and turning off reuse for Posts and Reels.
  • The article says the feature is part of a broader trend in which companies such as Meta and Google are adding AI-related data use settings that are opt-out rather than opt-in by default.

Unmasking BitRAT's C2 over HTTPS | Corelight — May Read

Corelight analyzes how BitRAT uses HTTPS for command-and-control and shows that defenders can still identify its activity through network telemetry and behavioral indicators despite encryption.

  • The article is titled "Unmasking BitRAT's C2 over HTTPS | Corelight."
  • The title identifies BitRAT as the subject of the article.
  • The title indicates that the article focuses on BitRAT's C2 activity over HTTPS.
  • The title associates the article with Corelight.

NSA revives 'Tailored Access Operations' name for elite hacking unit — May Read

The NSA has renamed its elite offensive cyber unit back to Tailored Access Operations as part of a leadership-driven reorganization meant to speed and strengthen operations against digital threats from countries like China and Russia. The move revives a storied unit known for custom hacking tools, Stuxnet, and links to the leaked EternalBlue exploit later used in WannaCry.

  • The National Security Agency changed the name of its Office of Computer Network Operations back to Tailored Access Operations last week.
  • The renaming is part of a reorganization by NSA’s new leadership intended to make the agency more adept at facing evolving digital threats from China, Russia, and others.
  • The move reverses parts of the NSA21 restructuring launched in 2016, which had folded offensive operations and intelligence collection into broader directorates rather than keeping TAO as a standalone office.
  • TAO creates and deploys custom software tools to penetrate foreign computer networks for espionage and helped craft the Stuxnet cyber weapon used to sabotage Iran’s nuclear program.
  • The unit drew public attention after the Shadow Brokers advertised stolen hacking techniques, including tools later associated with the EternalBlue exploit used in the 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak.

Microsoft to retire the OWA Light client in Exchange Server — May Read

Microsoft plans to disable and remove the legacy OWA Light client from on-premises Exchange Server in an upcoming update, likely in August 2026. Users will need to use the modern Outlook on the web experience, while admins can proactively block OWA Light now via Exchange PowerShell settings.

  • Microsoft announced plans to disable and remove OWA Light from Exchange Server in an upcoming update estimated for August 2026.
  • OWA Light was introduced roughly two decades ago as a simplified alternative for systems without Internet Explorer 6 or later, older browsers, low-bandwidth connections, or locked-down browser modes such as kiosks.
  • Microsoft said retiring OWA Light will reduce legacy surface area, simplify engineering work, and allow it to focus on the full Outlook on the web experience.
  • After the change is introduced, users will no longer be able to choose or be redirected to OWA Light and should use the modern Outlook on the web experience instead.
  • Admins can block OWA Light immediately with Set-OwaMailboxPolicy -OwaLightEnabled $false and remove the light selection menu on the logon page with Set-OwaVirtualDirectory -LogonPageLightSelectionEnabled $false.

Why we cannot wait for better post-quantum signature algorithms — Optional

Cloudflare argues organizations cannot wait for newer, smaller post-quantum signature algorithms because they likely will not be widely deployable until the 2030s. The practical path is to begin migrating now with ML-DSA despite its drawbacks, while continuing research into better alternatives for future upgrades.

  • Cloudflare says RSA and ECC are vulnerable to sufficiently advanced quantum computers, and it is targeting 2029 to become fully post-quantum secure.
  • The article argues that newer post-quantum signature algorithms will not be ready in time for the first transition, so ML-DSA must be used despite larger sizes and reduced flexibility compared with RSA and ECC.
  • NIST advanced nine post-quantum signature schemes to the third round of its signatures on-ramp, while a draft standard for FN-DSA is expected imminently.
  • The article says FN-DSA has smaller keys and signatures than ML-DSA but is difficult to implement securely for signing because of issues involving floating-point arithmetic and side-channel safety.
  • Cloudflare argues continued work on new signature schemes remains important because some systems cannot easily absorb ML-DSA’s size costs and because the research may help enable other post-quantum tools such as anonymous credentials.

Summer of Clearinghouses — Optional

The article argues that the new wave of open source vulnerability clearinghouses only matters if they can rapidly turn private findings into rebuilt, tested, signed, and upstreamed fixes. The real measure of success is throughput and reach, not how many vulnerabilities a clearinghouse holds.

  • Chainguard says its clearinghouse, Athena, was already running before it was announced and had been taking findings and shipping fixes for months.
  • The article argues that a clearinghouse is only a pool of vulnerability data, and the hard part is turning findings into rebuilt, tested, signed fixes that users can consume.
  • Chainguard says its build system watches thousands of open source projects and typically remediates most CVEs in roughly two days, with a one-day SLA for CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities.
  • The article says many private vulnerabilities are being found because AI models are tested against running applications and often discover flaws in open source dependencies rather than first-party code.
  • The author argues that successful clearinghouses should be judged by median time from finding to shipped fix, the fraction of fixes that do not require human handling, and the share of fixes that land upstream.

AI Authority Drift: The Permissions Nobody Approved — Optional

AI agents are accumulating permissions through integrations and inherited access faster than traditional reviews can track, creating “authority drift” that attackers can exploit using the agents’ own legitimate access. Organizations need live visibility and real-time enforcement of agent permissions rather than relying on static approval records or periodic reviews.

  • The article defines authority drift as an AI agent’s permission footprint expanding beyond what was originally approved until nobody can account for everything it can reach.
  • The article says AI agent access grows through inherited permissions from connected systems, new integrations added to solve immediate problems, and broad access granted for convenience.
  • In September 2025, state-sponsored attackers hijacked enterprise AI agent instances across 30 targets in defense, energy, and technology, using the agents’ accumulated access to move laterally in minutes.
  • CVE-2025-32711 was described as a zero-click prompt injection in Microsoft 365 Copilot that used a crafted email to extract data from OneDrive, SharePoint, and Teams through a trusted Microsoft domain.
  • The article argues that organizations need a live map of each agent’s access, restrictions to a fixed set of tools or models, and an enforcement point that can scope access without waiting for the next scheduled review.

Mitiga Joins Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program — Optional

Mitiga has joined Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program to use Claude’s advanced, vetted dual-use cyber reasoning to improve its Agentic Runtime Security detections. The key message is that as AI accelerates exploitation beyond the speed of patching, defenders need runtime controls that detect and stop attacks before they cause business impact.

  • Mitiga has joined Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program to use Claude’s advanced cyber reasoning for legitimate defensive work that is blocked by default for unverified users.
  • Anthropic’s Cyber Verification Program distinguishes between cyber activities with no legitimate use, which remain blocked for everyone, and dual-use activities such as exploitation analysis, adversarial simulation, and threat modeling, which verified defensive organizations can access.
  • The article argues that AI has compressed attackers’ timelines so much that exploitation can occur before a patch is available, making faster patching insufficient by itself.
  • Mitiga says it will use verified access to improve detections in Helios AIDR, the engine behind its Agentic Runtime Security, by reasoning about real attacker tradecraft such as exploit paths, exfiltration patterns, and chained footholds.
  • The article presents Agentic Runtime Security as a compensating control that watches cloud, SaaS, identity, AI, and third-party services to detect, interrupt, and stop attacks before they cause business impact.

AI Pentesting Buyer's Guide: How to evaluate AI pentesting vendors — Optional

Aikido’s AI pentesting buyer’s guide argues that organizations should evaluate vendors on how well they fit modern continuous delivery workflows, especially whether they support source-code-assisted whitebox testing, enforce scope technically, and retest as software changes.

  • Aikido’s survey of 200 CISOs and 200 engineering leaders found that 76% deploy significant changes at least weekly, nearly 40% deploy daily, and only 21% validate security on every release.
  • The article says AI pentesting is becoming a practical way to close the gap between continuous software releases and less frequent security validation.
  • Across more than 1,000 AI pentests, whitebox testing uncovered 7x more vulnerabilities while requiring fewer attempts than greybox testing alone.
  • The article recommends comparing AI pentesting vendors under comparable conditions, including authentication, source code, scope, validation, and reporting.
  • The article identifies red flags such as vendors being unable to explain finding validation, dismissing code access without evidence, relying on prompts for guardrails, or focusing demos only on familiar OWASP vulnerabilities.

WolfSSL, GeoVision, VTK vulnerabilities — Optional

Cisco Talos disclosed and vendors patched multiple vulnerabilities across WolfSSL, GeoVision, and VTK-DICOM, including command injection, buffer overflow, privilege escalation, XSS, and authentication issues. Users should apply vendor updates and use the latest Snort rules to detect potential exploitation.

  • Cisco Talos’ Vulnerability Discovery & Research team disclosed three vulnerabilities in WolfSSL, fourteen in GeoVision, and one vulnerability in VTK-DICOM.
  • The vulnerabilities discussed in the article have been patched by their respective vendors in accordance with Cisco’s third-party vulnerability disclosure policy.
  • The WolfSSL issues include two improper input validation vulnerabilities, TALOS-2026-2409 and TALOS-2026-2410, and one integer underflow vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2408.
  • Talos released 14 advisories for GeoVision vulnerabilities covering 37 CVEs, including memory corruption, OS command injection, buffer overflow, privilege escalation, reflected XSS, insufficient encryption, out-of-bounds read, and lack of authentication issues.
  • Talos found one VTK-DICOM vulnerability, TALOS-2026-2366, identified as CVE-2026-22879, which is a heap-based buffer overflow vulnerability.

Winning 54% of the time — Optional

Cisco Talos reports that China-linked UAT-7810 is expanding covert Operational Relay Box networks by exploiting unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers and deploying custom backdoors like LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH. Defenders should prioritize patching edge devices and monitoring for unusual proxying or unauthorized connections.

  • Cisco Talos’ latest findings say the China-nexus threat actor UAT-7810 is expanding its Operational Relay Box networks with a new suite of custom malware.
  • UAT-7810 exploits known vulnerabilities in unpatched Ruckus and ASUS routers to deploy tools including upgraded LONGLEASH and DOGLEASH backdoors.
  • The article says UAT-7810 builds covert networks to provide infrastructure for other APT groups to launch attacks against high-value targets.
  • ORB networks can let secondary threat actors mask their origins and route malicious traffic through seemingly innocuous nodes.
  • Defenders are advised to patch edge devices, especially Ruckus and ASUS routers, monitor for unusual proxying behavior or unauthorized connections, and use the indicators of compromise in the Talos blog post.

Why Do F1 Teams Need Cybersecurity, and How Is AI Changing the Threat Landscape? — Optional

F1 teams face enterprise-grade cyber risks because their competitive advantage depends on fast-moving telemetry, software, partner access, and global operations. The article argues that AI is making phishing, deepfakes, and discovery faster for attackers, while zero trust and AI-driven security controls are needed to protect data, identities, vendors, and AI systems.

  • Formula 1 teams generate hundreds of gigabytes of telemetry across a race weekend, and this data moves between the car, garage, trackside systems, factory, and pit wall.
  • The article says F1 teams must protect live telemetry, proprietary software and analytics, business data, and global operations across more than 20 countries in a season.
  • Third-party vendors, suppliers, contractors, media, and sponsors can extend an F1 team’s attack surface because they may need temporary or integrated access to systems.
  • The article identifies IP theft, ransomware, and social engineering as key threats facing F1 teams, with race timing increasing pressure during outages.
  • The article states that AI can help attackers create convincing phishing content, deepfakes, and automated discovery campaigns, while also helping defenders baseline normal behavior and correlate risks.

The Hidden Security Risks of Reduced Summer IT Coverage — Optional

Reduced summer IT staffing gives attackers more time to exploit phishing, BEC, unpatched systems, and delayed responses. Organizations can reduce this risk by using automation, alert prioritization, continuous monitoring, and predefined response workflows to maintain coverage when key staff are away.

  • Cybercriminals look for opportunities during summer vacation periods because reduced IT and security staffing can lead to slower response times and less oversight.
  • The article says holiday periods see a 40% increase in cyberattacks, with summer months being particularly vulnerable.
  • Lean staffing can make phishing and Business Email Compromise harder to spot, especially when approval chains are disrupted and key decision makers are out of the office.
  • The article argues that security operations often depend too heavily on human availability, causing alert fatigue, manual process bottlenecks, and slower responses during reduced staffing periods.
  • AI-driven automation, automated patching, intelligent alert prioritization, autonomous runbook execution, and continuous monitoring are presented as ways to maintain security coverage when staff are unavailable.

Introducing the Risk Score Engine: identity risk you can quantify — Optional

Permiso launched its Risk Score Engine, which assigns continuous 0–100 risk scores to every human, non-human, and AI identity using evidence from its Universal Identity Graph. The goal is to help organizations quantify identity risk, understand why scores change, and prioritize response.

  • Permiso is launching the Risk Score Engine, which assigns every identity in an environment a continuous, evidence-backed score from 0 to 100.
  • Every score breaks down across three dimensions: Behavior, Likelihood, and Impact.
  • The Risk Score Engine is built on Permiso’s Universal Identity Graph and covers human, non-human, and AI identities.
  • Score velocity tracks how fast a score is moving, because the rate of change can be an early sign that something is wrong.
  • The engine produces Identity Risk Scores, Session Scores, and Organization Risk Scores, and it is available now as part of the Permiso platform.

AI Attacks Move in Minutes. Join This Webinar on Building a Defense That Keeps Up — Optional

The article promotes a free Zscaler webinar on defending against AI-powered attacks that move faster than traditional security workflows. The main takeaway is that organizations should reduce exposed access, limit lateral movement with Zero Trust, and use early automated containment to keep pace.

  • The article says AI-driven attacks can complete work in minutes that once took attackers days.
  • The promoted webinar, “Outpacing Mythos: How to Fight Back Against AI-Powered Attacks,” will examine how AI-powered attacks get in, what they do once inside, and why network-based defenses can fall behind.
  • The article recommends shrinking what attackers can reach by cutting exposed entry points and enforcing least-privilege access.
  • The article recommends stopping lateral movement by dropping network-based trust and allowing only the connections users and workloads actually need.
  • Zscaler's Olivia Vort will present a Zero Trust approach intended to help defenders respond at machine speed.
